name: Garlic Compound Butter
method: Soften the butter to room temperature.

Slice into 25 g discs. Hold refrigerated up to 5 days.

Sear in olive oil, 3 minutes each side for medium rare.
Rest 5 minutes. Top with a 25 g disc of garlic butter.
Roast the potato, blanch the broccoli and glaze the carrot.
Warm the demi glace, finish with cream, nap the plate.
Plate the steak on the sauce, vegetables to the side.
Garnish with a rosemary sprig. Serve immediately.

name: Beef Curry

Heat the oil in the tilting pan. Fry the onions on medium heat until deep golden. This is the base of the whole dish, so do not rush it or the gravy will taste raw.
Add the ginger, garlic, green chilli and curry leaves. Fry for 2 minutes until the raw smell goes.
Add the turmeric, coriander, curry powder and red chilli. Fry for 60 seconds in the oil only - if the pan is dry, add a ladle of water so the spices bloom instead of burning.
Whisk the yoghurt smooth and stir it in off the boil, then bring back slowly. Adding it to a fiercely boiling pan will split it.
Stir in the tomato and cook until the oil separates and rises to the surface.
Add the beef and seal it in the masala, then let it braise in its own juices for 15 minutes before any water goes in. This is where the depth comes from.
Add the potato once the beef is already part-tender, or it will collapse before the meat is done.
Add the water, bring to the boil, then drop to a simmer. Cook until the potatoes are tender and the gravy has thickened to a coating consistency.
Correct the salt at the end, not the start - the gravy reduces and concentrates as it cooks.
Hold above 63 C for service. Record the batch temperature and the time it was made.

method: Pick over the whole green mung beans and wash in several changes of water until it runs clear.
Soak for at least 4 hours. Whole mung keeps its skin, so it needs longer than split.
Heat the oil, fry the onions to a deep golden, then add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and fry until the raw smell goes.
Add the turmeric, curry powder, coriander and chilli powder. Fry for a minute so the spices bloom.
Add the tomato and cook until the oil separates.
Add the drained pulses and the water. Bring to the boil, skim the foam, then simmer until soft and breaking down. Stir the base often - pulses catch and scorch easily in a large pan.
Adjust the consistency with hot water. If mashed potato flakes are on the card, whisk them in at the end to thicken; they will not dissolve properly in a cold or boiling pan.
Season, then hold above 63 C for service.

name: Mixed Dhal(Chana, Dal, lentil ,Chick peas)
method: Pick over the mixed pulses and wash in several changes of water until it runs clear.
Soak the chana and yellow lentil together for 4 hours. Keep the red lentil separate and add it later - it cooks in a fraction of the time and will disappear completely if it goes in at the start.
Heat the oil, fry the onions to a deep golden, then add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and fry until the raw smell goes.
Add the turmeric, curry powder, coriander and chilli powder. Fry for a minute so the spices bloom.
Add the tomato and cook until the oil separates.
Add the drained pulses and the water. Bring to the boil, skim the foam, then simmer until soft and breaking down. Stir the base often - pulses catch and scorch easily in a large pan.
Adjust the consistency with hot water. If mashed potato flakes are on the card, whisk them in at the end to thicken; they will not dissolve properly in a cold or boiling pan.
Season, then hold above 63 C for service.

name: Plain Paratha
method: Mix the flour, salt and sugar. Beat the egg into the water and add gradually, working to a soft dough.
Knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic, then rest covered for at least 30 minutes. Skipping the rest gives you a dough that fights back and tears when rolled.
Divide and ball the dough, brush with oil, and rest again for 15 minutes.
Roll out thin, oil the surface, then pleat and coil each one to build the layers.
Rest the coiled balls one more time before the final roll, then cook on a hot dry griddle.
Press the edges as it cooks and brush lightly with oil. Turn once each side is spotted brown.
Stack wrapped in a clean cloth to keep them soft - uncovered they go leathery within minutes.

name: Chapati Roti
method: Mix the flour and salt, then add the water gradually and work to a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth, work in the oil, then rest covered for at least 30 minutes.
Divide, ball, and roll out thin and even. An uneven roll will not puff.
Cook on a hot dry griddle until the surface bubbles, turn, then press the edges so it balloons.
Stack wrapped in a clean cloth. Serve warm.

name: Custard
method: Slake the custard powder and sugar in the cold water until completely smooth with no lumps.
Bring the milk to a gentle simmer, stirring so it does not catch on the base.
Pour the slaked mix into the simmering milk in a steady stream, whisking constantly.
Cook out for 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens and loses the raw starch taste. Under-cooked custard tastes chalky.
Take off the heat and stir in the rose water once it has stopped bubbling.
Portion hot into the service cups, then cool rapidly to below 5 C. Cover only once cold or condensation will thin the surface.

name: Jello
method: Bring the measured water to the boil.
Whisk in the jelly powder until every grain has dissolved. Any undissolved powder settles and sets as a gritty layer.
Portion straight away while still liquid - it starts to set as it cools.
Chill below 5 C for at least 4 hours until firmly set. Do not freeze; freezing breaks the gel and it weeps on thawing.

name: Mouhalabia
method: Slake the corn flour and sugar in the cold water until smooth.
Bring the milk to a gentle simmer, stirring constantly so it does not scorch.
Pour in the slaked corn flour in a steady stream, whisking hard to keep it lump free.
Cook out for 3 minutes until thick and glossy. Corn flour needs to boil to reach full thickness and lose its raw taste.
Off the heat, stir in the rose water and blossom water.
Portion hot, cool rapidly to below 5 C, and garnish before service.

name: Vermicelli Kheer Sweet (Dessert file)
method: Break the vermicelli into short lengths and fry in the ghee over low heat until evenly golden. It colours very fast at the end, so keep it moving and take it off early.
Reconstitute the milk powder with warm water and whisk until completely smooth with no lumps.
Bring the milk to a gentle simmer. Do not boil hard - reconstituted milk catches on the pan base and scorches.
Add the fried vermicelli and cook until soft, stirring often.
Add the sugar only once the vermicelli is soft. Sugar added early keeps the starch from swelling properly.
Slake the corn flour in a little cold water and stir it in to thicken. Cook out for 2 minutes.
Add the raisins and crushed cardamom, take off the heat, then stir in the rose water. Rose water is volatile - added over heat, the aroma boils away.
Cool rapidly to below 5 C if it is being served cold. Do not leave it standing warm.

name: Halawa semolina Indian
method: Dry roast the semolina in the ghee over low to medium heat until it is evenly golden and smells nutty. This is the longest step and it cannot be hurried - pale semolina makes pasty halawa.
Separately dissolve the sugar in the water with the saffron colour and bring to the boil.
Reconstitute the milk powder with warm water and whisk smooth, then add it to the syrup.
Pour the hot liquid into the roasted semolina slowly, standing back - it will spit violently.
Stir constantly until the grain swells and the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan.
Fold in the raisins and cardamom, then the rose water off the heat.
Spread into trays, level, and cool before cutting into portions.

name: Tang Juice
method: Dissolve the sugar in a small amount of hot water first, then top up with the remaining cold water. Sugar tipped into cold water sinks and takes a long time to dissolve.
Whisk in the juice powder until fully dispersed with no clumps on the surface.
Taste and adjust - powder strength varies between batches and flavours.
Chill below 5 C and serve cold in the cups. Portion close to service; the colour fades if it stands.

name: Tea -Black
method: Bring the water to a rolling boil.
Add the tea powder and simmer for 3 to 5 minutes. Stewing it longer draws out tannin and turns the brew bitter.
Strain out the leaf as soon as the colour is right - leaving it in means the tea keeps strengthening in the urn.
Stir in the sugar while hot until fully dissolved.
Hold above 65 C and serve in the paper cups.

name: Tea -Black with Milk
method: Bring the water to a rolling boil, add the tea powder and simmer 3 to 5 minutes.
Strain out the leaf, then stir in the sugar while the tea is hot.
Reconstitute the milk powder separately with warm water and whisk until completely smooth.
Add the milk to the strained tea and bring back to just below the boil. Adding milk powder directly to the tea leaves it lumpy and it will not strain out.
Hold above 65 C. Do not boil hard once the milk is in or it will catch and taste scorched.
Serve in the paper cups with a spoon.
